lessons.title: How data-driven improvement and DMAIC work
lessons.summary: You will be able to explain what data-driven improvement tries to do, calculate a defect rate as DPMO, and walk a problem through the five DMAIC phases.
lessons.why: Many clients in medical devices and pharma run improvement programmes and talk in Six Sigma terms: 'the Define phase', 'our Cpk', 'a Green Belt project'. If you join such a project to add data or AI, you need to speak that language and follow the method, because the method is how the client will judge whether your fix really worked. It also gives you a disciplined way to avoid jumping to a solution before the problem is understood.

p: Six Sigma is a method for improving a process by reducing variation and defects, using data rather than opinion. It grew out of manufacturing work at Motorola in the 1980s and spread to many industries. The core belief is simple: if a process gives a slightly different result every time, some of those results will fall outside what the customer accepts. Reduce the variation and you reduce the defects.

Sigma is the Greek letter statisticians use for standard deviation, a measure of how spread out results are. A process 'at six sigma' is so consistent that its limits sit far from the average. The figure usually quoted is 3.4 defects per million opportunities, which includes an allowance for the process average drifting over time.

sections.h: Variation: why the average is not enough
p: Every process varies. Two vials filled on the same machine a second apart will not weigh exactly the same, and two reviewers will not take exactly the same time on the same batch record. Some of that variation is small, random and built into the process. Some comes from a specific cause, such as a worn part, a new material lot or a skipped step.

Averages hide this. A filling line can hit its target weight on average while some vials are overfilled and others underfilled. The customer does not receive the average; each patient receives one vial. That is why Six Sigma measures spread as well as the centre, and why most of its tools aim to find what drives the spread and reduce it.
This course is internal learning that follows the Green Belt body of knowledge. Completing it is not an external belt certification; bodies such as ASQ run their own exams for that.

A defect is any result that does not meet a requirement. An opportunity is each place a defect could happen. A printed label might have four opportunities: product name, lot number, expiry date and barcode. One label with a wrong expiry date is one defect, even though the other three fields were right.

DPMO (defects per million opportunities) lets you compare processes of different complexity. You divide defects by total opportunities, then multiply by one million. The short script below shows the calculation for an example line.

code.text:
units = 500            # labels inspected (example)
opportunities = 4      # fields that could be wrong per label
defects = 18           # wrong fields found

total = units * opportunities
dpmo = defects / total * 1_000_000
print(f"Opportunities: {total}")
print(f"DPMO: {dpmo:,.0f}")
# Opportunities: 2000
# DPMO: 9,000

p: Six Sigma uses belt names for roles. A Champion is a manager who sponsors the project, removes blockers and owns the business result. A Black Belt leads larger projects and coaches others; it is often a full-time role. A Green Belt leads smaller projects or works on a Black Belt's team while keeping their normal job. Team members are the people who do the work in the process every day, and they usually know more about it than anyone else.
Professional bodies such as ASQ (the American Society for Quality) publish a body of knowledge for each belt and offer certification exams. Companies also run their own internal belt programmes.
DMAIC is the five-phase road map for improving an existing process. Each phase ends with a short review, often called a tollgate, where the Champion checks the work before the team moves on.
list: Define: state the problem, the customer and the goal in a one-page project charter. Draw a high-level process map, often a SIPOC (suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers).
Measure: decide what to measure, check the measurement system can be trusted, collect data and set the baseline performance.
Analyze: use data and tools such as a fishbone diagram, Pareto chart and hypothesis tests to find and prove the root causes.
Improve: design, test and pilot solutions that remove the proven causes, and confirm with data that performance improved.
Control: lock in the gain with updated procedures, training, control charts and a response plan, then hand the process back to its owner.

sections.h: Six Sigma in a regulated company
p: In a medical device or pharma company, Six Sigma does not run beside the quality system; it runs inside it. A DMAIC project started from a recurring complaint is often linked to a CAPA record. Any change made in the Improve phase to a validated process, a procedure or equipment must go through change control, and may need revalidation before it is used for product. The Control phase usually ends with revised, approved procedures and training records.
For new products or processes there is a related road map, DMADV (define, measure, analyze, design, verify), often grouped under the name Design for Six Sigma. DMAIC is for fixing what exists.

example.title: Worked example: missing lot numbers on a device label (example scenario)
p: A device plant finds that some shipping labels are printed with a blank or wrong lot number. Every one is caught at final inspection, but rework costs time and a missed one could block traceability in a recall. A Green Belt runs a DMAIC project. All numbers below are example values.
Notice that the team did not start with a solution. Someone had suggested 'buy a new printer' in week one. The data showed the printer was not the cause.
list: Define: charter states the problem as label defects found at final inspection, goal to cut DPMO by at least half in three months, Champion is the operations manager.
Measure: the team checks that two inspectors judge the same labels the same way, then counts defects on 500 labels with 4 opportunities each and finds 18 defects, a DPMO of 9,000.
Analyze: a Pareto chart shows most defects are wrong lot numbers. Data shows they cluster after shift changes, when operators type the new lot number by hand.
Improve: a pilot pulls the lot number from the ERP work order by barcode scan instead of typing. After the change is approved through change control, a two-week pilot finds 2 defects in 500 labels.
Control: the label procedure is revised and approved, operators are trained, and a weekly control chart of label defects is added to the line's dashboard with a named owner.

practice.title: Run a mini DMAIC on your own process
practice.goal: Practise each DMAIC phase on a small process you control.
steps: Pick a small repeat process you do yourself, such as preparing a weekly report or making coffee for the team.
Define: write a three-line charter with the problem, the measure of success and the goal.
Measure: list the opportunities for a defect and record how many defects happen over the next five runs, then calculate DPMO with the Python script in this lesson.
Analyze: draw a simple fishbone of possible causes on paper and mark the one your data points to.
Improve and Control: write one change and one check you would keep doing so the gain lasts, and ask Claude to critique your plan.
practice.done_when: You have a one-page DMAIC summary with a charter, a DPMO number, a root cause and a control step.

pitfalls: Jumping to a solution in Define. Write the problem without naming the fix; the data decides the cause.
Trusting data before checking the measurement. If two inspectors disagree on what a defect is, the baseline is noise.
Changing a validated process during Improve without change control. In a regulated plant the pilot itself may need approval.
Ending the project without a Control plan. Without an owner and a check, the old defect rate returns.

lessons.title: Define: charter, customer and scope
lessons.summary: You will be able to write a one-page project charter with a measurable problem and goal, link it to customer requirements, draw a SIPOC and set a scope the team can finish.
lessons.why: Most failed improvement projects fail in Define, not in the statistics. The team chases a problem nobody measured, or a scope so wide it never ends. As an FDE you are often asked to 'add data' or 'add AI' to a project that has no clear problem statement. Knowing how a good charter looks lets you ask the right questions on day one and stops you building a tool for the wrong problem.

p: Define is the first DMAIC phase. Its job is to agree what problem the team is solving, for which customer, how success will be measured and what is out of bounds. The main output is the project charter: a one-page document that the Champion signs before any data work starts.

A charter is a contract between the team and the sponsor. It protects the team from scope creep and protects the business from a project that drifts for a year. In a regulated company it is also evidence. If the project is linked to a CAPA or a complaint trend, the charter shows auditors why the work started and what it aimed to change.

A problem statement says what is wrong, where, since when, how big it is and why it matters. It describes the gap, not the cause and not the fix. 'Operators make mistakes on labels' blames people and guesses a cause. 'Over the last 13 weeks, 1.8 percent of shipping labels on Line 3 failed final inspection, causing rework and a risk to lot traceability' is a usable problem statement.

A goal statement says how much the measure should move and by when. Use the same metric as the problem statement so the result is easy to judge: 'Reduce label failures on Line 3 from 1.8 percent to below 0.5 percent by the end of the quarter, without adding inspection steps.' Many teams use SMART as a check: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound.
If you cannot fill in the number yet, write 'baseline to be confirmed in Measure' rather than inventing one. A charter is a living document and is updated at each tollgate.

sections.h: Voice of the customer and CTQs
p: The voice of the customer (VOC) is what customers say they need, in their own words. Customers can be external, such as a hospital or a patient, or internal, such as the warehouse that receives your labels. Sources include complaints, service records, interviews, surveys and returned product.

Customer words are usually vague: 'labels must be readable'. A CTQ (critical to quality) requirement turns that need into something you can measure, with a target and limits. 'Readable' might become 'barcode grade C or better on every label, and lot number matching the batch record'. The path is need, then driver, then CTQ. Each CTQ later becomes a measure in the Measure phase.

A SIPOC is a one-page, high-level map of the process. The letters stand for suppliers, inputs, process, outputs and customers. Fill it in this order: name the process, list its 4 to 7 main steps, then the outputs and customers, then the inputs and suppliers. Keep it high level. The detailed step-by-step map comes later.

The SIPOC does three jobs. It agrees where the process starts and stops, it shows which inputs could cause the problem, and it names the people who must be involved. In a regulated plant it also shows which records, systems and validated equipment sit inside the scope.

A good test of a SIPOC is to show it to someone who works in the process every day. If they cannot recognise their own work in the five or so steps, or they name an input you missed, fix the map before the tollgate.
list: Suppliers: who provides the inputs, such as ERP, the label stock vendor or the previous shift.
Inputs: what goes in, such as the work order, label template, printer and ribbon.
Process: the main steps from start trigger to end point.
Outputs: what comes out, such as the printed and applied label and the batch record entry.
Customers: who receives the outputs, such as final inspection, the warehouse and the end user.

p: Scope says what is in and what is out: which line, which products, which sites, which time period. An in-and-out list is the simplest tool. A Green Belt project should be small enough to finish in a few months by a part-time leader. If the problem spans many sites and systems, split it or pass it to a Black Belt.
List the stakeholders: the Champion, the process owner, the people doing the work, quality, validation, IT and anyone whose approval is needed for a change. Note what each needs to know and when.

The Define tollgate is a short review with the Champion. The team shows the charter, the SIPOC, the CTQs and the stakeholder list. The Champion agrees, asks for changes or stops the project. Stopping a weak project here is a good outcome, not a failure.

example.title: Worked example: a charter for late batch record review (example scenario)
p: A tablet plant releases batches late because batch record review takes too long. Quality says the reviewers are slow. A Green Belt is asked to fix it. All numbers are example values.
The first draft of the problem statement said 'reviewers need an electronic tool'. That names a fix. The team rewrote it as a gap with a number, then built the rest of the charter around it.
list: Problem: over the last 6 months, the median time from batch completion to QA release was 9 working days against a target of 5, delaying shipments.
Goal: median release time of 5 working days or less within 4 months, with no increase in review errors.
VOC to CTQ: planning says 'we need batches on time', which becomes 'release within 5 working days for at least 90 percent of batches'.
SIPOC: suppliers are production and the lab; inputs are batch records and test results; outputs are released batches; customers are planning and distribution.
Scope: in scope are solid dose batches at one site; out of scope are the electronic batch record system replacement and other sites.
Tollgate: the Champion approves, and asks the team to add the lab manager as a stakeholder because test results are an input.

Using a different metric in the goal than in the problem, so at the end nobody can tell whether the project succeeded.
Setting a scope so wide that a part-time Green Belt cannot finish it in a few months.
Treating customer words as requirements without turning them into measurable CTQs with targets.
Leaving out quality, validation or IT stakeholders until Improve, then finding the change needs months of approvals.

lessons.title: Measure and basic statistics
lessons.summary: You will be able to pick the right type of data, describe it with mean, median, range and standard deviation, read a histogram, plan a simple sample, judge whether a measurement system can be trusted and state a baseline.
lessons.why: An FDE usually arrives with data skills, and the Measure phase is where those skills meet the shop floor. Clients will ask you to pull data from MES, LIMS or a spreadsheet and 'show the baseline'. If you do not check how the data was measured and sampled, you can build a confident chart on numbers that are mostly noise. Measure is where the project earns the right to trust its own numbers.

p: Measure turns the CTQs from Define into numbers. The team decides exactly what to measure and how, checks that the measurement system gives consistent answers, collects data with a sampling plan, and describes current performance. The output is the baseline: how the process performs today, stated in the same metric as the charter goal.

Write an operational definition for every measure. It says what is measured, with which instrument or system, by whom, when and how a result is recorded. 'Label defect' needs a definition, such as 'any field that does not match the batch record, or a barcode below grade C'. Without it, two people count two different things.

Continuous data is measured on a scale and can take any value in a range: fill weight in grams, seal strength in newtons, review time in hours. Discrete data is counted or sorted into categories: number of defects, pass or fail, which shift made the unit.

Prefer continuous data when you can get it. A pass or fail result tells you only that a unit was outside the limit. A weight tells you how far from target it was, so you can see a process drifting long before it fails. Continuous data also needs far smaller samples to detect the same change.

Discrete data still has a place. Complaints, deviations and late batches are naturally counted, and a defect rate or DPMO is the right metric for them. Just plan for larger samples, and record the reason or category for each defect so a Pareto chart can be drawn later.

Every data set has a centre and a spread. The mean is the average: add the values and divide by how many there are. The median is the middle value when the data is sorted; it is not pulled around by one extreme value, which makes it better for skewed data such as times and delays.

The range is the largest value minus the smallest. It is quick but uses only two points. The standard deviation uses every point: roughly, it is the typical distance of a value from the mean. Six Sigma cares more about spread than about the mean, because a process with a good average and a large spread still makes defects.

A histogram shows the shape. Values are grouped into bins and each bar shows how many fall in that bin. Many measured processes give a bell shape called the normal distribution, where about 68 percent of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 99.7 percent within three. Look at the shape before you use any test that assumes normality: two humps often mean two machines, shifts or materials mixed together.

code.text:
import statistics as st

# Fill weights in grams from one shift (example data)
w = [50.2, 49.8, 50.5, 50.1, 49.6, 50.3, 50.0, 49.9, 50.7, 50.2,
     49.7, 50.4, 50.1, 49.5, 50.0, 50.6, 50.2, 49.9, 50.3, 50.0]

print(f"n      = {len(w)}")
print(f"mean   = {st.mean(w):.2f}")
print(f"median = {st.median(w):.2f}")
print(f"range  = {max(w) - min(w):.2f}")
print(f"stdev  = {st.stdev(w):.3f}")  # sample standard deviation

# Text histogram with 0.3 g wide bins
lo = 49.4
for i in range(5):
    a, b = lo + i * 0.3, lo + (i + 1) * 0.3
    count = sum(a <= x < b for x in w)
    print(f"{a:.1f}-{b:.1f} | {'#' * count}")

p: You rarely measure everything, so you sample. A sampling plan says how many units, how often and how they are chosen. Random sampling avoids bias. Rational subgroups, such as five units in a row every hour, keep short-term variation inside a subgroup and let differences between hours show up. Record the time, shift, machine and lot with each value so you can stratify the data later in Analyze.

Measurement system analysis (MSA) asks whether the measurement itself adds too much variation. A gage R and R study has several operators measure the same parts several times without knowing which part is which. Repeatability is the variation when one operator measures the same part again. Reproducibility is the variation between operators. For pass or fail judgements, an attribute agreement study plays the same role.

A widely used guideline from the automotive MSA reference manual treats gage R and R under 10 percent of total variation as acceptable, 10 to 30 percent as possibly acceptable depending on use, and over 30 percent as not acceptable. Your client may have its own limits in a procedure; use those.

The baseline states current performance with enough data to be believed: the mean and standard deviation, or the defect rate or DPMO, over a stated period and sample. Note anything unusual during collection. The Champion signs off the baseline at the Measure tollgate, and the charter goal is updated if the real number differs from the first estimate.

When the data comes from a system such as MES, LIMS or ERP rather than a manual sheet, check it the same way. Confirm what the field really holds, whether rounding or default values were applied, and whether some records are missing. Pull a handful of records and compare them with the paper or screen source before you trust the extract.

p: A team is reducing overfill on a powder filling line where the label claim is 50 grams. All numbers are example values.

The first gage R and R on the check-weigher showed that operators zeroed the balance differently. After one short training and a written zeroing step, a repeat study passed. Only then did the team collect baseline data, five consecutive units every hour for two weeks, with time, shift and filling head recorded.

lessons.title: Analyze: finding and proving root causes
lessons.summary: You will be able to list possible causes with a fishbone and 5 whys, focus with a Pareto chart, look for relationships with a scatter plot, and use a t-test or chi-square test to confirm or reject a suspected cause.
lessons.why: In regulated companies the phrase 'root cause' appears in every deviation, complaint and CAPA, and inspectors read those records closely. Too many of them say 'operator error' or 'retrained staff' without proof. An FDE who can separate a hypothesis from a proven cause, and show the data behind it, makes the investigation stronger and stops the client fixing the wrong thing.

p: Analyze has two halves. First you open up: list every plausible cause without judging. Then you narrow down: use data to keep the few causes that really drive the problem, often called the vital few, and drop the rest. The output is a short list of proven root causes, each with the evidence that supports it.

Keep two words apart in your head and in your records: a hypothesis is a cause you suspect, and a root cause is a cause the data supports. A fishbone diagram is full of hypotheses. Only tests, comparisons and experiments turn a hypothesis into a root cause.

A fishbone diagram, also called an Ishikawa or cause and effect diagram, puts the problem at the head and groups possible causes along the bones. In manufacturing the usual groups are the 6 Ms: man (people), machine, method, material, measurement and mother nature (environment). Build it with the people who do the work; they know causes no data set holds.

The 5 whys asks 'why' again and again until you reach a cause you can act on. The number five is a guide, not a rule. Its weakness is that it follows one path and trusts each answer. Use it to explore, then check each link in the chain with data before you write it in a CAPA.

sections.h: Narrowing down: Pareto and scatter plots
p: A Pareto chart sorts defect categories from most to least frequent, with a line showing the cumulative percent. Often a small number of categories explain most of the defects, which tells the team where to look first. Make sure the categories come from one operational definition, and consider weighting by cost or severity: the most frequent defect is not always the most harmful.

A scatter plot puts one continuous variable on each axis, such as seal temperature and seal strength, one point per unit. A pattern that rises or falls suggests a relationship. The correlation coefficient, r, runs from minus 1 to plus 1 and measures how tightly the points follow a straight line. Correlation does not prove cause: both variables may be driven by a third, such as the time of day.

Stratification is the simplest tool of all and often the most useful. Split the same data by shift, machine, operator, material lot or product and compare the groups side by side. This is why Measure asked you to record that context. A defect rate that looks steady overall can hide one machine running far worse than the rest.

A hypothesis test asks: if there were really no difference, how surprising would this data be? The starting assumption of no difference is the null hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large when the null is true. Many teams use 0.05 as the cut-off: below it, they reject the null and treat the difference as real. Decide the cut-off before you look at the data.

Use a two-sample t-test to compare the means of continuous data from two groups, such as two sealer settings. Use a chi-square test to check whether two categorical variables are related, such as shift and pass or fail. The script below compares two settings. It computes the t statistic and estimates the p-value with a permutation test, which shuffles the group labels many times and counts how often chance alone gives a result as large.

Here the p-value comes out at about 0.07. That is above 0.05, so the data does not yet prove the settings differ. It does not prove they are the same either. The honest next step is more data or a planned experiment, not a conclusion.

code.text:
import random
import statistics as st

# Seal strength (N) from two heat-sealer settings (example data)
a = [41.2, 39.8, 40.5, 42.1, 40.9, 41.7, 39.5, 40.8, 41.3, 40.2]
b = [41.9, 40.6, 41.4, 42.3, 41.0, 40.8, 42.0, 41.6, 40.9, 41.7]

def welch_t(x, y):
    se = (st.variance(x) / len(x) + st.variance(y) / len(y)) ** 0.5
    return (st.mean(y) - st.mean(x)) / se

t_obs = welch_t(a, b)
print(f"mean A = {st.mean(a):.2f}, mean B = {st.mean(b):.2f}")
print(f"t = {t_obs:.2f}")

# Permutation test: how often does a random relabelling give a t this large?
random.seed(1)
pooled, hits, runs = a + b, 0, 10_000
for _ in range(runs):
    random.shuffle(pooled)
    if abs(welch_t(pooled[:10], pooled[10:])) >= abs(t_obs):
        hits += 1
print(f"p-value (approx) = {hits / runs:.4f}")

p: A cause is confirmed when the evidence is consistent from several angles: the data shows the link, the mechanism makes physical sense, and, where it is safe, switching the cause on and off moves the result. Record each confirmed cause with its evidence, and record the rejected hypotheses too. At the Analyze tollgate the Champion should see why each cause was kept or dropped, not just the final answer.

In a medical device or pharma company, this record usually feeds a deviation, complaint or CAPA investigation. Write each cause in plain words, link the data and analysis files, and say how confident you are. If the data cannot confirm a cause, say so and describe the interim control that protects product while the work continues.

example.title: Worked example: wrong lot numbers by shift (example scenario)
p: A label project found in Measure that most defects were wrong lot numbers. The fishbone listed many hypotheses, including printer faults, label stock, a confusing screen and shift changes. All numbers are example values.

The Pareto chart confirmed wrong lot numbers as the largest category. The team then counted labels with a wrong lot number on 400 labels from each shift. Day shift had 6 and night shift had 22. A chi-square test, shown below, gives a value of about 9.5, well above 3.84, the 5 percent critical value for a two by two table. Shift and defects are related.

That was still not the root cause. The 5 whys and a floor walk showed that night shift starts more new lots, and each new lot means typing the lot number by hand. The confirmed cause was manual entry at lot changeover, which the Improve phase could remove.

code.text:
# Labels with a wrong lot number, by shift (example data)
table = {"day": (6, 394), "night": (22, 378)}  # (defective, good)

rows = list(table.values())
col = [sum(r[i] for r in rows) for i in range(2)]
total = sum(col)
chi2 = 0.0
for r in rows:
    for i in range(2):
        expected = sum(r) * col[i] / total
        chi2 += (r[i] - expected) ** 2 / expected

print(f"chi-square = {chi2:.2f}")
# 3.84 is the 5 percent critical value for 1 degree of freedom (a 2 x 2 table)
print("shift and defects are related" if chi2 > 3.84 else "no evidence of a link")

sections.title: Improve: designing and piloting solutions
sections.summary: How to generate and select solutions for proven causes, mistake proof the process, run a small pilot, check new risks with an FMEA and pass change control before rollout.
outline: Change control and revalidation before rollout

lessons.title: Improve: designing and piloting solutions
lessons.summary: You will be able to generate solutions for each proven cause, choose between them with clear criteria, prefer mistake proofing over reminders, plan a small pilot, update an FMEA for the new process and explain why change control comes before rollout.
lessons.why: Improve is where FDE work often lands: a barcode scan instead of typing, an automatic check in a system, a data feed that removes a manual step. In a regulated plant even a good fix cannot simply be switched on. It has to be risk assessed, approved through change control and, where it touches a validated process or system, verified or revalidated. Knowing this path lets you design solutions that can actually be approved and used.

p: Improve takes the proven root causes from Analyze and removes or controls them. The team generates options, selects the best with agreed criteria, tests the choice on a small scale, checks what new risks it creates and then gets it approved before full use. The output is a piloted solution with data showing the gain, an updated risk assessment and an approved change.

Every solution should point back to a proven cause. If a proposed fix does not address any cause on the Analyze list, ask why it is in the plan. This one question removes many pet projects that have been waiting for a budget.

Keep the Champion close in this phase. Solutions cost money, change how people work and may need approvals from several functions, so the sponsor's support matters more here than anywhere else in DMAIC.

Start wide. Brainstorm with the people who run the process and ask, for each cause, how it could be removed, made impossible or detected sooner. Look at how other lines, sites or industries solved the same kind of problem. Write down even odd ideas; they often lead to a practical one.

Then select. A decision matrix lists the options as rows and the criteria as columns, such as effect on the cause, cost, time to implement, validation effort and risk. Each criterion gets a weight, each option a score, and the weighted total gives a ranking. The matrix does not make the decision, but it makes the reasons visible and stops the loudest voice in the room from winning by default.

In regulated work, validation effort is a real criterion. A change to a label template may need a short verification; a change to a sterilisation cycle may need a full revalidation. Two fixes with the same effect can differ by months in approval time.

Mistake proofing, or poka-yoke, designs the process so that an error is impossible, or is caught at once. It is stronger than training or a warning sign, because it does not rely on people remembering under pressure. Think of the stages in order of strength:
list: Prevent: the error cannot happen, such as a connector that only fits one way or a lot number pulled from the work order by scan.
Detect at once: the error is caught before the next step, such as a vision system that stops the line when a label is skewed.
Detect later: inspection finds the error downstream, which is weaker because the defect has already been made.
Warn: a sign, a checklist or retraining, the weakest control and the one most often overused in CAPAs.

p: A pilot tests the solution on a small scale before full rollout: one line, one shift, a few weeks. Plan it like an experiment. State what you expect to change, the measure and sample size, how long it will run and what result counts as success. Use the same operational definition and measurement system as the baseline, otherwise you cannot compare.

When several factors may matter, such as temperature, pressure and dwell time on a sealer, a designed experiment (DOE) changes them together in a planned pattern. It finds the effect of each factor, and how they interact, with far fewer runs than changing one factor at a time. A Green Belt should recognise when a DOE is needed; designing larger experiments is Black Belt territory.
In a regulated plant a pilot that makes product for sale is itself a change. It usually needs an approved protocol or a planned deviation and quality agreement before it starts.

Every fix changes the process, and every change can create new failure modes. Update the process FMEA (failure mode and effects analysis) for the new process. For each step, list how it could fail, the effect, and score severity, occurrence and detection, often from 1 to 10. Their product, the risk priority number or RPN, helps rank the work. Some newer FMEA methods replace the RPN with an action priority table. Either way, look at high severity items on their own, not only the ranking.

Before rollout, the change goes through the change control procedure in the quality system. Quality, validation, regulatory and the process owner assess the impact on validated processes, equipment, software, procedures, training and, where relevant, registered product details. FDA's process validation guidance describes validation as a lifecycle, so a significant change can send the process back for further qualification. Deciding the depth of revalidation for sterile, aseptic or complex processes is specialist work; this lesson gives awareness, not readiness to make that call.

example.title: Worked example: removing manual lot entry (example scenario)
p: The Analyze phase proved that wrong lot numbers came from typing the lot number by hand at lot changeover. All numbers are example values.

The team listed four options: a second-person check, a reminder sign, a drop-down list of open lots, and scanning the lot from the work order barcode. The decision matrix scored the scan highest on effect and only medium on validation effort, because the label software was already validated and the change was a new configured input. The sign and the second-person check scored low on effect because they rely on attention.

The updated FMEA, shown in the FMEA script in this lesson, ranks 'wrong lot typed' as the top risk before the change. After the change that failure mode no longer exists, but a new one appears: 'barcode scan misread'. The team added a check that the scanned lot matches an open work order. Change control approved a two-week pilot on one line under a protocol. The pilot found 2 defects in 500 labels against 18 in 500 at baseline, measured with the same inspection method. The change was then rolled out to the other lines after the software change was verified.

outline: Statistical process control and control charts

lessons.title: Control: making the gain last
lessons.summary: You will be able to write a control plan with a response plan, choose and read a simple control chart, list the documents and training that must change, and hand the process over to its owner with evidence that the gain holds.
lessons.why: Improvements fade when the project team moves on. Old habits return, a new operator never learns the new step, a setting drifts. FDEs often build the dashboards and alerts that sit in the Control phase, so you need to know what a control chart is really telling you, who must act on it and what the regulated quality system expects before a project can be closed.

p: Control is the last DMAIC phase. Its job is to make the improved process the normal process and to detect quickly if it slips. The team writes a control plan, sets up monitoring such as control charts, updates procedures and training, confirms the gain with data over a sustained period, and hands the process to its owner.

The test of a good Control phase is simple: if the whole project team left tomorrow, would the process owner know what to watch, what normal looks like and what to do when something goes wrong? If the answer is no, the project is not finished.

A control plan is a table that lists, for each critical input and output of the process, what is checked, how, how often, by whom and where it is recorded. It covers the CTQs from Define and the key causes proven in Analyze. If manual lot entry was the cause and the fix was a barcode scan, the control plan checks that the scan step is working, not only that the labels are right.

Each row needs a response plan: what the person does when the check fails or a signal appears. 'Inform the supervisor' is not enough. A good response plan says how to contain product, who is told, who decides and where the event is recorded. In a regulated plant this usually means linking to the existing deviation procedure, not inventing a new one.

Prefer controls that run themselves. A system check that blocks a wrong lot needs no one to remember it, while a manual audit depends on time and attention. Where a manual check is the only option, keep it short, make the record simple and put it at the point where the work is done, not in a separate report at the end of the week.

Every process varies. Statistical process control (SPC) separates two kinds of variation. Common cause variation is the normal, random noise of a stable process. Special cause variation comes from something specific and new: a worn tool, a new material lot, a missed step. The aim is to react to special causes and leave common cause noise alone, because adjusting a stable process in response to noise makes it worse.

A control chart plots a measure in time order with a centre line and upper and lower control limits. The limits are calculated from the process's own data, usually at three standard deviations of the plotted statistic from the centre. They are not specification limits. Specification limits come from the customer or the product requirements; control limits describe what the process is actually doing.

Pick the chart to match the data. An individuals and moving range (I-MR) chart suits one value at a time, such as one result per batch. An X-bar and R chart suits small subgroups, such as five units every hour. A p-chart tracks the proportion defective, and a c-chart tracks a count of defects per unit. The script below builds an I-MR style check from example data. It sets the limits from the first 15 days, then flags any day outside them.

code.text:
import statistics as st

# Daily label defects per 1,000 labels after the fix (example data)
x = [2.1, 1.8, 2.4, 2.0, 1.6, 2.2, 1.9, 2.5, 2.0, 1.7,
     2.3, 2.1, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 4.1, 2.0, 1.9]

base = x[:15]  # use the first 15 days to set limits
mr = [abs(base[i] - base[i - 1]) for i in range(1, len(base))]
center, mr_bar = st.mean(base), st.mean(mr)
ucl = center + 2.66 * mr_bar  # 2.66 = 3 / 1.128 for moving ranges of 2
lcl = max(0.0, center - 2.66 * mr_bar)
print(f"CL = {center:.2f}  UCL = {ucl:.2f}  LCL = {lcl:.2f}")

for day, v in enumerate(x, start=1):
    flag = "  <-- out of control, start the response plan" if not lcl <= v <= ucl else ""
    print(f"day {day:2}: {v:.1f}{flag}")

p: A point outside the control limits is the clearest signal. Other signals are patterns that random noise rarely makes, such as a long run of points on one side of the centre line (rules commonly use 8 or 9 in a row) or a steady trend up or down. Choose a small set of rules, write them in the procedure and train people on them. Too many rules cause false alarms and people stop reacting.
Recalculate limits only for a reason, such as a proven and approved process change. Do not widen limits because the process keeps breaking them; that hides the problem the chart was built to show.

Dashboards built by data teams often show a measure with a target line but no control limits. That tells you whether you met the target, not whether the process changed. Add the limits, or a link to the control chart, so the viewer can tell a real signal from normal noise.

Update every document the change touches: SOPs, work instructions, batch record templates, forms, system configuration records and the FMEA. In a regulated company these go through document control and are approved before use. Train the people who do the work, and keep training records, before the new procedure takes effect.

Confirm the gain with data over a sustained period, long enough to include normal changes such as shifts, material lots and staff rotation. Compare against the baseline with the same measure and measurement system.

Then hand over. The process owner signs that they accept the control plan, the monitoring and the response plan. The team writes a short closure report: problem, root causes, solutions, results against the goal, open actions and lessons learned. If the project was linked to a CAPA, the effectiveness check in the CAPA record should point to this evidence. The Champion closes the project at the Control tollgate.

example.title: Worked example: holding the label gain (example scenario)
p: After the barcode scan was rolled out, the label defect rate fell to about 2 per 1,000 labels. All numbers are example values.

The control plan had three rows: a daily check that the scanner rejects a lot that is not on an open work order, the daily defect rate per 1,000 labels on an I-MR chart, and a monthly audit of ten batch records. Each row named an owner and a response.

The Python block in this lesson shows the chart. Limits from the first 15 days were about 1.0 to 3.1. On day 16 the rate jumped to 4.1, outside the upper limit. The response plan said to hold the day's labelled stock, inform the line supervisor and quality, and open a deviation. The investigation found a replacement scanner had been fitted without the lot check enabled. The setting was corrected under change control, the held stock was inspected, and the next days returned inside the limits.

The team confirmed the gain over three months, updated the label SOP and training records, and the line manager signed the handover. The CAPA effectiveness check referenced the chart and the closure report.

sections.title: Process capability
sections.summary: How to judge whether a stable process can meet its specification, using Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk and sigma level, and how capability is used in validation and supplier quality.
outline: Cp and Cpk and what they tell you
Using capability in process validation and supplier quality

lessons.title: Process capability
lessons.summary: You will be able to tell specification limits from control limits, calculate and explain Cp, Cpk, Pp and Ppk, check the conditions that make them valid, and know where capability is used in validation and supplier quality.
lessons.why: Capability numbers travel far. They appear in validation reports, supplier scorecards, management reviews and sometimes in submissions. A Cpk calculated on unstable or non-normal data can make a weak process look safe. FDEs who build quality dashboards or analyse batch data are often asked to 'add Cpk'. You need to know when the number means something and when it should not be shown at all.

p: Process capability compares what the process does with what the specification allows. The specification is the voice of the customer: the lower and upper specification limits (LSL and USL) a product must meet. The process spread is the voice of the process. A capable process fits its natural spread comfortably inside the specification, with room to spare.

Capability only makes sense for a stable process. If a control chart shows special causes, trends or shifts, the process has no single predictable spread, and any capability index describes the past rather than the future. Check stability first, then capability. This order is the most important idea in this lesson.

Specification limits come from requirements: a product specification, a drawing, a registered limit or a customer agreement. They say what is acceptable. Control limits come from the process's own data and say what the process normally does. The two have nothing to do with each other in the calculation.

A process can be in control and still not capable: stable, but its normal spread is wider than the specification, so it makes a predictable share of defects. It can also be capable but out of control: today's results are inside specification, but special causes mean you cannot predict tomorrow. You want both: in control and capable.
Because of this, keep the two kinds of limits on separate visuals, or label them very clearly when they share a chart. Operators react to control limits; release decisions use specification limits.

Cp compares the width of the specification with the width of the process spread, taken as six standard deviations: Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 x sigma). Cp of 1 means the process spread just fills the specification. Cp of 2 means the specification is twice as wide as the spread. Cp ignores where the process is centred.

Cpk adds centring. It measures the distance from the mean to the nearer specification limit, in units of three standard deviations: Cpk = min(USL - mean, mean - LSL) / (3 x sigma). If the process is perfectly centred, Cpk equals Cp. If it drifts towards one limit, Cpk falls. A Cpk below 1 means part of the natural spread lies outside the specification.

Many companies set a minimum Cpk in their procedures, often 1.33 for existing processes and sometimes higher for critical characteristics. Use the client's procedure, not a number from a website. Some teams also quote a sigma level, which for a centred, normal process is roughly three times Cpk.

Sample size matters too. An index from 20 values carries much more uncertainty than one from 100, and two calculations on different small samples can differ a lot. Always state the number of values and the period with the index, and be careful comparing lines or suppliers on small samples.

Which sigma you use matters. Within-subgroup sigma captures short-term variation, estimated for example from the average moving range divided by 1.128. Overall sigma is the ordinary standard deviation of all the data and includes drift between shifts, lots and days. Cp and Cpk usually use within sigma and describe potential capability. Pp and Ppk use overall sigma and describe the performance customers actually received.

A big gap between Cpk and Ppk is a finding in itself. It means the process could do well in the short term, but something shifts it over time. The script below shows that case. The example data drifts steadily upwards: Cp and Cpk look excellent at about 2.4, while Pp and Ppk are about 1.4. The right reaction is not to report the higher number. It is to find and remove the drift, then recalculate on stable data.

code.text:
import statistics as st

# Tablet weight in mg, one value per batch in time order (example data)
x = [249.6, 249.9, 249.5, 250.1, 249.8, 250.2, 250.0, 250.4, 250.1, 250.6,
     250.3, 250.8, 250.5, 251.0, 250.7, 251.2, 250.9, 251.4, 251.1, 251.5]
lsl, usl = 248.0, 253.0  # specification limits (example)

mean = st.mean(x)
mr_bar = st.mean(abs(x[i] - x[i - 1]) for i in range(1, len(x)))
s_within = mr_bar / 1.128     # short-term spread
s_overall = st.stdev(x)       # long-term spread

def indices(s):
    p = (usl - lsl) / (6 * s)
    pk = min(usl - mean, mean - lsl) / (3 * s)
    return p, pk

cp, cpk = indices(s_within)
pp, ppk = indices(s_overall)
print(f"mean = {mean:.2f}  s_within = {s_within:.3f}  s_overall = {s_overall:.3f}")
print(f"Cp = {cp:.2f}  Cpk = {cpk:.2f}")
print(f"Pp = {pp:.2f}  Ppk = {ppk:.2f}")

p: The formulas above assume the data is roughly normal. Many real measures are not: impurity levels, particle counts, times and anything near a natural limit of zero tend to be skewed. On skewed data the normal formulas can be badly wrong in the tail, which is exactly where defects live. Options include fitting a suitable distribution, transforming the data, or using a percentile method that replaces the six sigma spread with the distance between the 0.135 and 99.865 percentiles. Look at a histogram and a normality check before choosing.

Capability is used widely in regulated work. Many companies set capability expectations in process validation protocols and in continued process verification, which FDA's process validation guidance describes as stage 3 of the validation lifecycle. Supplier quality agreements often require capability data for critical dimensions or attributes. Setting acceptance criteria and sample sizes for validation, and handling non-normal data in a validation report, is specialist statistical work that should be reviewed by a qualified statistician. This lesson builds understanding, not readiness to sign that work off.

example.title: Worked example: tablet weight before a supplier review (example scenario)
p: A quality engineer is asked for the Cpk of tablet weight for a quarterly review. The specification is 248 to 253 mg and there are 20 batch results in time order. All numbers are example values, the same as the script in this lesson.

A first calculation gives Cpk of about 2.4, which would look excellent on a slide. Before reporting it, the engineer plots the data on an individuals chart and sees a steady upward trend from 249.6 to 251.5 mg. The process is not stable. The overall-sigma Ppk of about 1.4 is closer to what was really delivered, and if the drift continues the mean will approach the upper limit.

The engineer reports the trend instead of a single index, with both numbers and a note that capability cannot be claimed until the drift is explained. The investigation finds gradual wear on a press tooling set. After the tooling is replaced under the maintenance procedure and new stable data is collected, capability is recalculated and reported with the sample size and period.
